title: What is IAM, and what is the difference between an IAM User, an IAM Group, an IAM Role, and an IAM Policy?
shortTitle: IAM: User, Group, Role and Policy
keyPoints: IAM (Identity and Access Management) controls who is authenticated and what they are authorized to do in an AWS account.
An IAM User is a permanent identity with long-lived credentials such as a password or access keys, meant for a human or legacy application.
An IAM Group is a collection of Users that share the same policies, used purely for convenience and never as a login identity.
An IAM Role is an identity with no permanent credentials that is assumed temporarily to receive short-lived credentials from STS.
An IAM Policy is a JSON document that lists allowed or denied actions on specific resources and is attached to Users, Groups, or Roles.
Effective permissions are the union of all attached policies, minus any explicit deny which always wins.
Roles are preferred over Users for machines because temporary credentials reduce blast radius if leaked.

s1_definition.oneliner: User is a permanent person, Group bundles people for shared rules, Role is a temporary borrowed identity, and Policy is the rulebook that grants the actual permissions.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **IAM (Identity and Access Management)** – The AWS service that controls authentication (who are you) and authorization (what may you do) for every request to every AWS service.
- **IAM User** – A permanent identity with long-lived credentials (password and/or access keys) for a human or legacy application.
- **IAM Group** – A collection of Users that share the same policies, used only for convenience; you never log in as a Group.
- **IAM Role** – An identity with no long-lived credentials, assumed temporarily through STS to obtain short-lived credentials that expire.
- **IAM Policy** – A JSON document listing allowed or denied actions on specific resources, attached to Users, Groups, or Roles to grant permissions.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, an IAM User is a permanent staff member like Rajesh with his own ID card and password. An IAM Group is a department like Tellers – everyone in it automatically gets the teller permissions. An IAM Role is a temporary visitor badge: a contractor or a machine borrows it for a few hours, does the job, and the badge expires. An IAM Policy is the printed rulebook that says exactly which rooms a badge can open – may open the cash vault, may not open the manager's office.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
┌─────────────────── AWS Account ───────────────────┐
│                                                    │
│  IAM User (Rajesh)                                 │
│  ├── Console password + MFA                        │
│  ├── Member of Group: NBI-Developers               │
│  │   └── Policy: ReadStatements                    │
│  └── Inline Policy: WriteTransfers                 │
│                                                    │
│  IAM Role (SettlementServiceRole)                  │
│  ├── Trust Policy: EC2 can assume this role        │
│  └── Permission Policy: ReadWriteStatements        │
│       │                                            │
│       ▼                                            │
│  EC2 Instance (Settlement Service)                 │
│  └── Instance Profile → Role                       │
│      └── SDK auto-fetches temporary credentials    │
│          from instance metadata (169.254.169.254)  │
│          └── Credentials expire in 1 hour          │
│              └── SDK auto-refreshes before expiry  │
│                                                    │
│  Policy Evaluation Flow:                           │
│  Request → Gather all policies                     │
│         → Explicit Deny? ──YES──→ DENIED           │
│         → Explicit Allow? ─YES──→ ALLOWED          │
│         → Neither? ─────────────→ DENIED (implicit)│
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
IAM is the AWS service that answers two questions for every request: who are you, and what are you allowed to do. The four building blocks are User, Group, Role, and Policy, and the key is understanding which ones are identities and which one is the permission itself. A Policy is the permission – a JSON document that says allow or deny a set of actions on specific resources. It carries no identity on its own; you attach it to something.

A User is a permanent identity with long-lived credentials, meant for a human or a legacy application that needs its own password or access keys. A Group is not something you log in as; it is a bundle you attach policies to once and then add Users into, so twenty engineers who need the same access all inherit it from one place and a single edit updates them all. A Role is the one people misunderstand most – it is an identity with no permanent credentials that is assumed temporarily through STS, handing back short-lived credentials that expire in about an hour.

The reason Roles matter so much in banking is security. At National Bank of India our statement-generator service runs on EC2 and needs to read the customer-statements bucket. If we embedded an access key in that code and it leaked through a log or a repository, an attacker could use it until a human noticed and rotated it. Instead the EC2 instance assumes a Role, receives temporary credentials automatically, and those credentials rotate on their own, so there is simply no long-lived secret to steal.

The way I explain the effective permissions in an interview is this: a User's permissions are the union of its own inline policies plus every policy on every Group it belongs to, and then any explicit deny overrides everything. If nothing allows the action, the implicit deny applies. So in our setup engineers get read access by being in the Developers group, the service gets the same read access through an assumed Role with no keys in the code, and the policy itself is written once and reused everywhere, which is exactly how you keep a bank's access model both secure and maintainable.

Remember one sentence: User is a permanent person, Group bundles them, Role is a temporary badge for machines and cross-account access, and Policy is the JSON rulebook that actually says Allow or Deny.
